question.text: 'Vikramaditya AIF' is being incorporated as a Company under the Companies Act 2013 — the least preferred route. Which of the following is a MAJOR constraint of the Company structure that makes it inferior to trust/LLP?

answer.text: Companies cannot issue units, only equity shares, making unit-class waterfalls impossible
Companies cannot offer limited liability to investors
Companies cannot appoint an investment manager
Companies are restricted to a maximum of 200 investors under private placement rules, vs 1000 permitted for an AIF scheme

explanation.text: The Logic: The company route for an AIF is least preferred because compliance is cumbersome and the Companies Act private-placement cap permits not more than 200 investors. AIF Regulations, by contrast, permit up to 1,000 investors per scheme with accredited investors excluded from the count. This binding 200-versus-1,000 cap is the defining structural constraint. The Trap: Option A overstates the share/unit issue; companies can use differential equity rights. Option B is false because all three pool alternatives — trust, LLP and company — provide limited liability. Option C is false; companies can appoint an investment manager. Note: Source pages 131 and 137 support the 200-investor private placement cap, the 1,000-investor AIF scheme cap with accredited investors excluded, and the cumbersome compliance critique.
